content.title: About
content.content: Beef Egg Foo Yung is a Chinese‑American dish consisting of an omelette filled with strips of beef, vegetables, and seasoned with soy sauce. It originated in the United States in the 1970s and quickly became a staple in Asian‑fusion restaurants.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish blends the traditional Chinese egg‑foo‑yung technique with the American addition of beef.
Original recipes often use soy sauce, sesame oil, and scallions for flavor.
It is commonly served over rice or noodles, and sometimes with a side of fried potatoes.
In the 1970s the dish became a symbol of cultural exchange between China and the United States.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Beef and eggs provide complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Beef supplies easily absorbed heme iron, supporting healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and beef are good sources of B12, niacin, and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: A modest amount of monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats contributes to heart health.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Contains selenium and vitamin E, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Egg whites can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Soy sauce adds significant salt, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Beef quality
items.content: Improperly cooked or low‑quality beef may harbor harmful bacteria.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish can be calorie‑rich due to oil and meat; portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the beef egg foo yung hot, sliced into bite‑size pieces. It is eaten with a fork and knife, often accompanied by steamed rice, noodles, or a vegetable side.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. Reheat with a splash of oil or sauce to restore moisture.

pasta-whole-grain-with-cream-sauce-and-a.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Cream Sauce and Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pasta with cream sauce and added vegetables is a restaurant (3667) dish made from whole‑grain pasta, a smooth cream sauce, and fresh vegetables. The whole‑grain pasta retains bran and germ, making it more nutritious, while the cream sauce gives the dish a velvety texture and mild flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain pasta provides more fiber and micronutrients than regular white pasta.
The cream sauce is often made with a blend of cream and low‑fat milk to reduce calories in restaurant (3667).
Vegetables may include broccoli, spinach, bell pepper, and zucchini, boosting vitamin and antioxidant content.
The dish is served hot, frequently topped with grated Parmesan or oregano for extra aroma.
Whole grain pasta has a lower glycemic index, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Whole grain pasta contains soluble and insoluble fiber that supports healthy digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The vegetables add vitamin C, vitamin K, folate, and potassium, while the pasta contributes iron and magnesium.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Because of the whole grain, the dish raises blood glucose more slowly, which is beneficial for weight management and diabetes control.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: The cream sauce, prepared with a touch of olive oil, provides monounsaturated fats that support heart health.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Broccoli, spinach, and bell pepper contain carotenoids and polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The cream sauce may contain dairy, which can cause discomfort for people with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Whole grain pasta contains gluten, making the dish unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The creamy sauce adds significant calories; portion control is advisable for those watching weight.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Added salt in the sauce can increase sodium intake; individuals with hypertension should ask for reduced salt.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, tossing it with the sauce and vegetables. Garnish with fresh basil, grated Parmesan, or nuts for extra texture. It can be paired with a light mixed‑green salad if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. When reheating, add a splash of water or milk to keep the sauce from becoming too thick.

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese pizza on a gluten‑free thin crust is a variation of the classic pizza made with a wheat‑free dough, making it suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity. The crust is crisp, and the cheese (usually mozzarella) adds a smooth, creamy flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Gluten‑free dough is often made from rice, corn, or potato flour.
A thin crust yields a crunchier bite compared with traditional thick crusts.
Mozzarella cheese, commonly used on pizza, originates from Italy and is traditionally made from water buffalo milk.
Pizza gained widespread popularity in the United States after World War II when Italian immigrants opened the first pizzerias.
Gluten‑free pizza options became widely available only in the 2010s due to growing demand for gluten‑free products.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: The cheese provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Mozzarella is rich in calcium, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: Lower carbohydrate content
items.content: Gluten‑free thin crust typically contains fewer carbs than traditional wheat dough, which can help with blood‑sugar management.

items.title: Rich flavor with less added fat
items.content: A thin crust allows for less oil and sauce while still delivering a satisfying taste.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or dairy protein allergy.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Cheese and sauce can be high in salt; choose low‑sodium versions if you monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Even with a thin crust, pizza can be calorie‑dense due to cheese and oil; portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Reheat the pizza in a 200 °C oven for 5‑7 minutes to restore crispness. Slice into bite‑size pieces and serve with a green salad or fresh vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftover pizza in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in a freezer‑safe bag for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before eating.

potato-salad-with-egg-made-with-mayonnai.title: Potato Salad with Egg, Made with Mayonnaise

content.title: About
content.content: Potato salad with boiled eggs and mayonnaise is a classic dish of Russian cuisine. Boiled potatoes and eggs are diced, mixed with mayonnaise, salt and pepper. Often chopped green onion, dill or a touch of mustard is added for extra flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The salad is a staple on holiday tables, especially for New Year and Victory Day.
The first published recipe for potato‑egg salad appeared in Soviet cookbooks in the 1930s.
Traditional Soviet mayonnaise was homemade from egg yolks, vegetable oil and vinegar.
Regional variations may include mustard, pickles or boiled carrots.
The salad keeps well in the refrigerator for 3‑4 days.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Eggs and potatoes provide complete proteins essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs are rich in B2, B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potatoes supply potassium, important for heart and muscle function.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Mayonnaise made with vegetable oil delivers monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: If the salad includes potato skins, it adds fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg proteins.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Mayonnaise makes the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight management.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Salads containing raw eggs should be kept refrigerated and not left at room temperature for more than 48 hours.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Excessive salt can contribute to elevated blood pressure.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled as a side dish or appetizer alongside meat dishes. It can be eaten with a spoon or used as a sandwich filling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C. After 3 days the texture and flavor may start to decline.

rice-white-with-gravy-no-added-fat.title: Rice, white, with gravy, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Rice, white, with gravy, no added fat is boiled white rice served with a light sauce prepared without oil or butter. The dish is often used in diet plans because it provides minimal fat while delivering a quick source of energy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice is one of the most widely consumed grains worldwide.
When cooked properly, rice retains most of its carbohydrates but virtually no fat.
Fat‑free gravy is usually made from broth, tomatoes, or aromatic spices.
Rice appears in traditional dishes across Asia, Europe, and the Americas, adapted for low‑fat diets.
Compared with whole‑grain rice, white rice has a softer texture and cooks faster.

items.title: Fast energy source
items.content: White rice is rich in carbohydrates that quickly convert to glucose, providing immediate energy.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: A fat‑free preparation makes the dish suitable for low‑fat dietary regimens and helps control calorie intake.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Boiled rice is gentle on the stomach, making it appropriate for people with sensitive digestion.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Rice provides thiamine (B1), niacin (B3) and folate, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Supports hydration
items.content: Cooked in water, rice retains moisture that contributes to overall fluid balance.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Low fiber content
items.content: Unlike whole‑grain rice, white rice provides little dietary fiber, which may affect digestive health.

items.title: Possible arsenic content
items.content: In some regions rice can accumulate arsenic; choose reputable sources to minimize exposure.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the rice as a side dish with vegetables, lean fish, or poultry. Add the fat‑free gravy just before serving to preserve flavor. Fresh herbs, lemon juice, or spices can be added for extra taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked rice should be cooled quickly and kept in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat to at least 75 °C before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Yellow rice is processed rice that is cooked with added fat (usually vegetable oil or clarified butter) and spices such as turmeric or saffron, which give it a characteristic golden colour and aroma. The product is ready to eat and is commonly used as a side dish for meat, fish, and vegetable meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Yellow rice is traditionally prepared in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, and South Asian cuisines.
Adding fat increases the calorie density, making the dish more satiating.
Turmeric, often used for coloring, has anti‑inflammatory properties.
Saffron, though expensive, imparts a vivid golden hue and a unique fragrance.
In many cultures yellow rice is served on festive occasions as a symbol of abundance.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The carbohydrates provide quick glucose for the body’s energy needs.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Rice contains thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: The added vegetable fat supplies monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Antioxidant properties of turmeric
items.content: Turmeric’s curcumin acts as an antioxidant and anti‑inflammatory agent.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Easily digestible rice can be gentle on the stomach and suitable for low‑fiber diets.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Added fat raises the calorie count, so portion control is important for weight management.

items.title: Spice allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to turmeric, saffron, or other added seasonings.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Prepared versions may contain salt; people with hypertension should check sodium content.

items.title: Gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: Manufacturing facilities may also process gluten‑containing foods, which is relevant for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve yellow rice hot as a side dish with meat, fish, vegetable stews, or legume dishes. It can be used in salads, casseroles, or as a base for pilaf. Add fresh herbs, a squeeze of lemon, or toasted nuts for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked yellow rice in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze portions in bags at –18 °C or lower. Reheat to at least 75 °C before serving.
